paras: The Hoisington warning notices were typewritten notices posted around Hoisington, Kansas, one night in late September or early October 1903, warning the town's Black residents to leave. A rumored attempt to enforce them on the following Monday night passed without any disturbance, and the episode is known from a single local news item.

According to the Hoisington Dispatch, "several notices written on a typewriter were posted up around town one night last week warning the negroes to leave town." The item did not say who posted the notices, what prompted them, or how many Black people lived in the town. Talk then spread that "an attempt would be made to enforce the notices Monday night," but the paper reported that "no disturbance was made."
The coverage names no suspects and reports no arrests, investigation or official response. It also does not say whether any Black residents left Hoisington because of the warnings.

The report reached print through the Barton County Democrat of Great Bend, which on 9 October 1903 ran a column of Hoisington news credited "From The Dispatch." The two sentences on the notices came last in a run of routine local items, after news of a surprise party, the roofing of the new school house and Sunday services at the opera house. The item carried no headline of its own and offered no comment on the notices or on the people they targeted, whom it called "the negroes."
No other report of the notices, and no follow-up, was found in either the white or the Black press, so this brief item remains the only account.
